An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

It has been revealed that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she says. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that blueprint, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

According to recent reports, on the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

According to recent reports, he’s killing my kids, she mentioned, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

Recent findings suggest that her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

In a recent development, it was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

She did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Industry observers note that still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The plan was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

Two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

She discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up swiftly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

She could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

According to recent reports, karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage company where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

Karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

To understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

In a recent development, her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, big laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

She bought the gown at one of those massive bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

Recent findings suggest that the newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

In a recent development, david had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

After the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Industry observers note that why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

Recent findings suggest that some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

Recent findings suggest that also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

It was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

Sources indicate that that startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

According to recent reports, she pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

According to recent reports, the fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

It has been revealed that how he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

Karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

Halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Industry observers note that then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

Was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

In a recent development, the texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

It has been revealed that her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

Recent findings suggest that from what Karen can piece together, it seems his blueprint was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

Was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

Sources indicate that the fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

On November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Industry observers note that karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

Somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Major Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who showed up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

Industry observers note that it took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

She’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she prepares to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

In a recent development, most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

It will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she says, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

Before “cloud” was associated with On’s trainers and Phil Knight cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports, which eventually became Nike, there was Asics. The brand was founded over 75 years ago as Onitsuka Tiger, and would eventually merge with the Asics Corporation in 1977. The Asics “tiger stripes” logo on its shoes derives from the 1950s Onitsuka Tiger Mexico 66 shoe model. Its Gel-Cumulus and Gel-Nimbus legacy models were released in 1999.

Though the manufacturer is Japanese, the origin of Asics’s name is actually a Latin acronym, anima sana in corpore sano, for “sound mind in a sound body.” This ethos is exemplified when wearing, running, and racing in an Asics shoe. The brand’s dynamic cushioning provides comfort and a responsive ride for all running experiences. Well-received by wear-testers, we’ve included Asics trainers in multiple buying guides, including Best Running Shoes and the 2026 Shoe Awards.

Runner’s World has offered running advice and gear recommendations since 1966. We assembled a 300-plus-runner local group of varying experience levels, paces, and foot types to test the latest shoe releases and give their honest assessments on fit, comfort, and ride.

Sources indicate that the shoes included on this list were all vetted by wear-testers and RW staff. I have also included my own experience testing some of these models during all kinds of workouts and in a couple of races.

RW contributor Michael Charboneau provided insight on Asics shoe tech and answered frequently asked questions about Asics trainers.

The Novablast 6 gets an injection of fun that is awfully reminiscent of the original. For this revision, though, Asics cored out a hole in the forefoot and filled it with A-TPU, a foam that’s bouncier than PEBA. The effect is that the carrier (the bulk of the midsole) delivers a predictable, stable ride, yet the forefoot feels explosive and propulsive. It makes this everyday trainer suitable for days when you want to pick up the pace.

“The Asics Novablast 6 is a bouncy do-it-all shoe that excels with faster paces,” mentioned tester and Runner’s World Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Compared to other up-tempo daily trainers I’ve tested, like the. New Balance Rebel v5 and Nike Pegasus 42, it has more cushion and a softer feel, yet is still light and bouncier than both.”.

Testers liked the reworked knit upper, improved AsicsGrip rubber outsole, and responsive trampoline pod of FF Turbo Squared foam in the forefoot.

The GT-2000 underwent a makeover with its 14th iteration. Asics has carried these changes over to the GT-2000 15, ensuring the cushioning feels even softer with an added 2 mm of FF Blast Max foam. According to recent reports, the Gel-Cumulus is a long run favorite for its plush, supportive cushioning. It buffers miles of pounding in a surprisingly lightweight package. The shoe’s midsole is FF Blast Max, which promotes soft landings with high rebound. The foam—along with Asics’s PureGel tech—provides arch support for both neutral runners and underpronators.

Since its release 27 years ago, the Gel-Nimbus has delivered a premium cushioned, long-lasting ride. The Gel-Nimbus 28 is updated with 20 grams shaved off its weight, a feature testers were keyed in on when they ran in the shoe.

Year after year, the Gel-Kayano lands on our list of the best stability shoes for its comfortable fit and smooth ride. The latest version introduces Asics’s new stability tech: FluidSupport.

Replacing the 4D Guidance System, which made the shoe feel stiff, FluidSupport enhances cushioning with a dual layer of foam. FF Blast Plus and FF Blast Max are combined in the midsole; what you get is a softer top layer of foam and a denser bottom layer. Working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry, FluidSupport provides guidance only when you need it.

The result is a more flexible trainer that delivers high energy return on your runs.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Industry observers note that the Magic Speed 5 is the cheaper but still capable carbon-fiber-plated racing shoe for the first-time marathoner or 26.2 vet looking for a speedwork trainer. FF Blast Plus foam cushions your landings along with a layer of the brand’s lightest and bounciest FF Leap foam. Asics also reduced the offset to 7mm and the heel height and forefoot height for a more stable ride.

Recent findings suggest that testers felt the shoe was too firm for long runs, but liked its responsiveness for shorter efforts during their training. Midfoot striker Gabrielle Kelenyi, who trains at 7:45 pace, said the Magic Speed 5 wouldn’t be her first choice of shoe in terms of comfort (the arch felt too pronounced for her foot), but the functionality was there.

The lace closure was secure. Overall, I wore these for shorter runs (6 miles) and they gave those runs some extra oomph. They were not comfortable enough for longer runs (8+ miles).”.

Other testers, like Stephanie Petrides, appreciated the arch support and overall cushioning.

According to recent reports, “I have very flat feet and tend to give my knees and ankles a good pounding because of it, but the cushioning made everything very comfortable,” mentioned Petrides, an overpronator. “The shoe was definitely not too soft and didn’t make me feel like it was slowing me down.”.

Recent findings suggest that I raced in the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at the 2025 Sydney Marathon and didn’t expect to run 3:05 after combatting a week of being a tourist and jet lag. Sources indicate that “I think the increased padding on your foot is the biggest improvement from previous models. I think I also love it because it still feels like a normal shoe but just with some enhancement of the speed.”.

Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo Review.

The Sonicblast is your prep shoe before showtime, or that trainer with just a little more oomph when you want to push the pace during workouts. A Pebax Astroplate is sandwiched between 46mm of FF Blast Max and FF Turbo Squared foams, to stabilize the ride as the shoe propels you forward. FF Turbo Squared is Asics’s high-performance A-TPU foam, which delivers aggressive rebound.

Testers loved the bouncy, high energy return ride and praised the shoe’s supportive cushioning.

“The best part of the shoe was the ride of the shoe for me,” said tester Tegan Kovacs, who’s been using the Sonicblast 2 for structured long runs. “It was very comfortable and honestly just plain fun! The shoe was comfortable and foamy enough to take on longer distances, and delivered a propulsive ride when you kicked it up a notch.”.

While testers like the Sonicblast 2’s propulsive ride, some were wary of sharp corners due to the shoe’s tall stack height.

“I found that taking a turn does require a little more care to counter some of the instability of the higher stack height, but it wasn’t enough of a concern for me to worry too much about it,” remarked editor Ashley Tysiac. “Because the cushioning is much more firm rather than plush, I could still easily navigate a fork in the road or a turn on the greenway without feeling like I was going to turn my ankle.”.

The Blast series hits the trail. Testers loved the comfort the Blazeblast provided fit-wise and on the run. The shoe has FF Blast Max cushioning to provide a plush, high-energy-return ride. The trampoline pod outsole and midsole design promotes propulsion during toe-off.

The AsicsGrip outsole was satisfactory for our testers who ran the shoe on the road, towpaths, and semi-rocky terrain.

“The only shoe that I can kind of compare this to were the Hoka Mafate Speed 4,” stated tester Anna Piskorska. “Both of them are very light and have a great flexibility at the midfoot. The Asics give you enough cushion throughout the foot. There’s a noticeable bounce feeling, which allows you to rapidly lift off and pick up speed instantly.”.

Some testers wanted longer lugs for dicier trail efforts. “For a shoe with trail running as a mission, the tread is a bit lacking with the 2.5mm lugs as they will serve you well on mild inclines but anything wet or steep (or wet and steep!) is likely going to be troublesome,” remarked tester Eric Bartosz. “Just like my Kawasaki, it’s fine for some easy trails, but I would need to change tires for anything more demanding or technical...and that’s OK!”.

Still, testers appreciated how the Blazeblast made runs feel easier and faster off road.

Shop Men’s at asics.com | Shop Women’s at asics.com.

In a recent development, the Megablast has that high-octane, pogo stick bounce that makes it earn our Most Aggressive title. The shoe’s midsole is pure FF Turbo Squared, Asics’s bounciest foam. At a tall 46mm stack height, the Megablast is a lot of shoe at a surprisingly light weight.

Josh Davis, an underpronator who trains at 7:00 pace, described the shoe as bulky but appreciated its bouncy ride.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a pretty darn good shoe,” he stated. “The super high deck broadcasts the FF Turbo Squared foam, and it lives up to its name. For its size, the shoe is pretty darn light and very responsive. I’ve put over 100 miles on it at this point, and haven’t noticed any change in the pop. I liked this shoe for easy runs. I didn’t try to push it in any workouts because the shoe was a bit bulky.”.

Recent findings suggest that some testers, including myself, felt the ride was too squishy and erratic in a whole lot of shoe. RW contributor and tester Heather Mayer Irvine stated “the junk in the trunk” was her least favorite aspect of the Megablast.

Industry observers note that with the Superblast 3 you get the best of both worlds in terms of cushioning and ride. The midsole has FF Blast Plus foam and FF Leap on a trampoline pod-shaped sole, designed to encourage better toe-off.

Runners loved its soft but supportive foam and bounce. Stated intermediate runner and 7:45 pacer Erin Dewalt: “I like the combination of lightweight cushion and bounce most. For half marathon and marathon training, when you’re logging lots of miles, foot comfort is paramount. During my long runs, I’d marvel at how comfortable my feet felt even towards the end.”.

Nick Miller, an underpronator and heel striker, named the cushioning as his favorite Superblast 3 feature.

Industry observers note that “The cushioning of the Superblast 3 is what truly sets it apart from other shoes I’ve tested,” he remarked. “Its substantial stack height provides exceptional impact absorption, noticeably reducing the stress on my legs during runs. This made a clear difference on longer efforts, where fatigue typically builds up, and allows me to recover more promptly between sessions.”.

In a recent development, some testers, however, including myself, felt the loudness of the shoe was distracting. When I tested the Superblast 3 on my runs, the pavement slapping was comparable to Nike’s Alphaflys.

According to recent reports, asics has cooked up quite a few proprietary features, and you’ll see many different terms when browsing the firm’s running shoe lineup. To help you get more insight into these features, compare models, and find the right shoe, here’s a deeper dive on the main Asics running shoe tech to know.

This tech consists of a squishy, gel-like substance implanted in the midsole, and it absorbs impact forces for a smoother ride. The latest iteration is PureGel, and it’s formulated to be lighter, softer, and more flexible than previous versions of Gel.

Like other shoemakers, Asics has its own proprietary cushioning, called FlyteFoam (FF). Although it’s based on ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), the traditional running shoe cushioning material, this foam is formulated to be lighter and more resilient than standard EVA. It doesn’t have quite the same springy feel as the other types of FF below, but it works fine for everyday running. It’s used in Asics’s more affordable shoes.

According to recent reports, FF Blast Plus is the next level up. Asics hasn’t released details on the chemistry, but it likely includes olefin block copolymers, which make for a lighter, more flexible and more responsive foam. For a pillowy and springy ride that still holds up to everyday training, FF Blast Plus is the cushioning to go with.

Asics has also released an updated version, called FF Blast Max, that has a lower density, so it’s even softer and bouncier. It gives models a very plush ride. For maximum cushioning that doesn’t sacrifice responsiveness, look for training shoes with FF Blast Max.

It has been revealed that asics’s elite racing shoes have FF Turbo Plus foam. It’s made with polyether block amide (PEBA), an exceptionally light, soft, and bouncy material. The brand took this foam up a notch with the even bouncier FF Turbo Squared. Leap foam, which is made of Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU), is a super foam that’s softer and lighter than FF Turbo Squares. It is used in the brand’s top tier racing shoes. The shoes with this type of cushioning are pricey, but provide excellent shock absorption and springy responsiveness for a smooth, propulsive ride that helps you go fast. For race day, it’s definitely the top choice.

Industry observers note that asics takes a holistic approach to stability in its shoes, with several features working together to support the foot and guide it from landing to toe-off. The latest version of its stability feature-set is called the “4D Guidance System.” The 4D Guidance shoes feature a wide sole, a firm foam layer in midsole under the arch, and a flared sole shape at the heel to create a planted feel while counteracting overpronation, or excessive inward rolling motion in your step.

Sources indicate that some models have an earlier version of the system, called 3D Guidance. It has the same general features as 4D, but lacks the firm arch support foam in the midsole. If you know you need stability shoes, or simply prefer a more guided, supportive design, then you should look for these features.

Asics has developed a well-deserved reputation for manufacturing reliable shoes that can hold up through high-mileage training. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus, Gel-Nimbus, and Gel-Kayano have been around for decades (and continuously improved upon in that time), and they’re great picks if you’re looking for everyday trainers.

That noted, the brand has also expanded into lightweight, responsive racing shoes and even trail shoes, too.

How do Asics shoes compare to shoes from other brands?

Historically, Asics shoes have been known for using multiple layers of cushioning to create a stable, well-cushioned (and somewhat stiff) ride. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus still exhibit this construction, with a moderate drop and layers of Gel and foam in the midsole for a plush feel that’s great for long runs and training miles.

However, newer shoes in the Asics lineup, like the Novablast, utilize more lightweight, bouncy midsole designs that mirror what other top brands are doing in their premium speedwork and racing shoes.

Has Asics created any key innovations in running shoe tech?

According to recent reports, the short answer: Yes, lots of them. Asics has been experimenting with running shoe tech for well over half a century. In 1990, the brand opened the Institute of Sports Science in Kobe, Japan, where the manufacturer conducts materials tests and biomechanical research to fine-tune designs.

According to recent reports, this lab has produced and refined many of Asics’s hallmark technologies, like Gel cushioning and super foams, like FF Leap and FF Turbo Squared. For runners, this means Asics shoes are built with proven designs that can help you meet your goals, from sticking to a training plan to nabbing a new PR on race day.

She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

According to recent reports, if you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

Sources indicate that during our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what people had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

The rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most users would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

On the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

In a recent development, the frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review indicates, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state issues like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

It has been revealed that the NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

It has been revealed that A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

Sources indicate that if you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

Industry observers note that the ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H.

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage.

Display: 10-inch smart HD touchscreen.

According to recent reports, the NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

Recent findings suggest that the pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

In a recent development, what factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:.

It has been revealed that once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

According to recent reports, after measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

Industry observers note that rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Recent findings suggest that getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

According to recent reports, rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

According to recent reports, the machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

According to recent reports, the level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that A good pair of mountain bike shorts should stay out of your way through long climbs, rough descents, and everything in between. The right fit leaves room to pedal and wear knee pads without bunching or snagging, while a secure waistband and well-placed pockets keep the shorts comfortable on the trail. We’ve tested options for different budgets and riding styles, from lightweight shells to shorts with a padded liner. These are the pairs we’d choose for our next ride.

According to recent reports, the Pearl Izumi Summit Shorts scored well across the board, with a comfortable fit, effective water repellency, and well-placed pockets. At 191 grams, they’re relatively light and breathe well (though the Velocio Ultralight MTB Shorts below are yet lighter and more breathable). The Summits still move enough air for all-day trail rides without noticeable moisture buildup.

Their four-way-stretch ripstop nylon has held up through multiple seasons of testing and riding, resisting tears without feeling rough or abrasive. For nylon, it’s surprisingly soft.

A lined mountain bike short at this price is rare. The Ally has a forgiving fit and plenty of waist adjustment (Velcro sizing tabs and belt loops), which makes it easier to wear than many shorts. On the bike they feel relaxed and comfortable (but not floppy), and move with you well. The included liner means you don’t need to buy a chamois separately. Plenty of pockets let you stash a phone and ride essentials, though all those zippers can feel like a lot—and like potential failure points over time. The unisex sizing means there’s no separate women’s version.

Recent findings suggest that with a 13-inch inseam in the men’s version, the Landfarer covers the tops of most knee pads without feeling heavy. The stretch fabric is lightweight, and the broad range of men’s and women’s sizes makes it easier to find a good fit. Patagonia also uses recycled nylon in the fabric and makes the shorts in a Fair Trade Certified™ factory, so the vibes are good. The range of waist sizes can help you find a tailored fit, but the elastic waistband has no adjusters. The low-friction fabric and forgiving waist can let the shorts slip more easily, so make sure you get the right size.

The Ultralight lives up to its name. It’s extremely light and quick-drying, with a cut and fit dialed for long days with lots of pedaling. Despite the light material, these have proven surprisingly durable, shrugging off slides and brushes with rocks and trailside vegetation. I tested the latest version, which features a newly introduced elastic waist that greatly improved the fit and made it more forgiving of weight fluctuations. One caveat: that waistband change appears to be rolling through production, so not all pairs and colors have the new waist yet. These are also expensive.

Industry observers note that the Flexair keeps things low-key and streamlined. Its low-profile cut and ratchet closure make for a clean look and a secure fit on the bike. The leg opening sits close to the thigh, so these work best with very low-profile knee pads; bulkier pads may feel crowded. Stretch fabric and laser-cut perforations help keep the shorts light and ventilated, but there’s no liner. The waists run small, so try them on if you can and be prepared to size up.

Sources indicate that there are plenty of great bike shorts out there—but most of them play it safe with earth tones and muted colors. Wild Rye bucks that trend. This women-led brand out of Sun Valley, ID makes technical “apparel that inspires more women to get outside”—and look good doing it. The standout designs and bold colors are just as impressive as the performance of the gear itself. If you want high-quality apparel with flair and personality, this is your brand.

The Riley 10” Bike Short checks all the right boxes. A high-rise waist prevents sagging in the back while riding, and a stretch panel across the rear waistband adds comfort and flexibility. Along with a side zip pocket that fits a phone, the shorts also have two front pockets for smaller essentials. The 10-inch inseam will suit most riders, though it may not pair perfectly with all knee pads.

Pro tip: Check the sale page for deals on last year’s designs.

A company that builds only women’s athletic apparel typically nails it in every category, and these super-comfortable, breezy shell shorts from Shredly are no exception. With a versatile 11” inseam and a wide, high, soft waistband, these pair really well with a slightly longer chamois liner or waist shorts, and sit high on the waist to reduce gapping during rides.

Industry observers note that the shorts material has 9 percent spandex for structure and four-way stretch that lends maximum range of motion. These are built for a woman’s hips and waist, and have an articulated taper that doesn’t impede pedaling.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

The Best Protein Powders for Weight Loss, According to a Certified Nutrition Coach

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone notes they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat.
  • It has been revealed that protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation.
  • The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone notes they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed strategy in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

It has been revealed that protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

According to recent reports, this content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:.

I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

In a recent development, jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

Kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he indicates. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

Tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a substantial fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she says. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

Industry observers note that one thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a big investment.

In a recent development, I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is crucial for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

The taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

Kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he notes. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

This protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

Recent findings suggest that I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

Industry observers note that one thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

One of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

According to recent reports, along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”.

Sources indicate that naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and notes it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

If you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

It has been revealed that from a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

Tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he says. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”.

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:.

Protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

Choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

In a recent development, when you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

According to recent reports, it’s vital to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s crucial to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

According to recent reports, regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

Recent findings suggest that as a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

It has been revealed that whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

As a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s important to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

According to recent reports, protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

According to recent reports, weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

When focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

According to recent reports, there’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.
